sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the region to the northeast of the city of Reggio Emilia and belongs to the Ferrara Arc thrust front. This fault system is the NW-to N-verging external arc at the north-eastern tip of the Northern Apennines chain, well into the Po Plain, and marks the northeastern most advanced thrust with damaging seismogenic potential in the Apennines. This source has been updated within the research developed during the European Project GeoMol (http://www.geomol.eu/).
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a number of intermediate to damaging earthquakes that have affected the area; to the southwest, they are the 11 September 1831 (Mw 5.5, Reggiano), and 10 February 1547 (Mw 5.2, Reggio Emilia) earthquakes; to the south, the 20 June 1671 (Mw 5.3, Rubiera) event; to the north, the 12 February 1806 (Mw 5.3) and 25 Dec 1810 (Mw 5.3, Novellara) earthquakes, while the 15 October 1996 (Mw 5.4) has hit the southwestern sector of the source. Finally, a sparse intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) seismicity can be found in the whole region.
This Source is composed by the left ramp of the blind Ferrara-Romagna Apennines outer thrust and may account for the intermediate to damaging seismicity of the region. In particular, the 1806 and 1810 earthquakes are interestingly very close both in space and time, as it is not seldom observed in the seismic history of Italy and in its complex patterns concerning possible fault interaction. These two events may well have been caused by two adjacent segments (to date unknown) of this source.
To the southwest, this Source gives way to the Northern Apennines outer thrust.
The strike of this Source was based on that of the mapped buried structures. The dip was based on geological observations and geometrical considerations. The rake was chosen to represent pure thrusting, based on geological observations and the orientation of the structure. The minimum and maximum depth were based on tectonic and geometrical considerations concerning the thrust geometry. The slip rate calculated using geologic subsurface data from Maesano et al. (2015).

pictures.t: Tectonic map of the Northern Apennines thrust fronts
pictures.c: Structural map of the Northern Apennines thrust fronts showing a temporal reconstruction of their activity (from Castellarin et al. [1985]).

pictures.t: River anomalies and buried anticlinal axes in the Po Plain
pictures.c: Map showing the position of the main drainage anomalies in the Po Plain compared with the axes of buried anticlines of the Northern Apennines fronts (from Burrato et al. [2003]). The seismogenic source of the 1624 Argenta earthquake falls to the north of the anomaly nr. 22 related to the Idice River.

pictures.t: Vertical movements in the Po Plain near Mirandola
pictures.c: Summary of inferred Holocene vertical movements in the area of the Panaro, Secchio and Po rivers, near Mirandola (from Panizza et al. [1987]).

pictures.t: Paleochannels of the Po River and main tributaries
pictures.c: Recent evolution of the Po River and its main tributaries. The thrust fault driving the Mirandola anticline is likely responsible for the attraction of the Panaro and Secchia rivers towards the syncline north of Modena, while the Po River appears to be shifted northward (from Veggiani [1985]).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
